title: Swollen face and wheeze ten minutes after a first weight-loss injection

source.citation: Al-Rashid AH, Ali F. Suspected Biphasic Anaphylaxis Following the First Known Dose of Tirzepatide: A Case Report and Brief Review of Reported Hypersensitivity Reactions. Cureus. 2026;18(8):e113910.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Sudden facial swelling, hives and difficulty breathing
presentation.hpi: About 10 minutes after self-injecting her first-ever subcutaneous dose of tirzepatide 2.5 mg (prescribed for weight management) into her abdomen, she developed sudden facial and periorbital swelling, palpitations, nasal congestion, severe wheeze and chest tightness, followed by itchy wheals over her face, trunk and limbs and profound dizziness. The pen was new, intact and correctly stored. She has never used tirzepatide or another GLP-1 receptor agonist and denies recent exercise, infection, alcohol or any new food or medicine. She arrives about 30 minutes after symptom onset.
pmh: No atopy, asthma, chronic urticaria or previous drug allergy
meds: Tirzepatide 2.5 mg SC (first dose, 10 minutes before symptoms)
Combined oral contraceptive (ethinylestradiol 30 µg / drospirenone 3 mg) for 5 years
presentation.family: No family history of atopic or immunological disease.

exam: Widespread urticarial wheals over the face, trunk and limbs
At later review: small (2 × 2 cm) non-itchy erythematous plaque at the abdominal injection site

diagnosis.primary: Anaphylaxis after the first dose of subcutaneous tirzepatide (skin, respiratory and cardiovascular involvement; WAO criteria), with a suspected biphasic reaction

management: Rapid IV infusion of 1 L 0.9% sodium chloride and IM epinephrine 0.3 mg (1 mg/mL) into the left anterolateral thigh
Nebulized albuterol 2.5 mg, ipratropium 0.5 mg and budesonide 1 mg

Hypotension and respiratory compromise persisted at 5 minutes: second IM epinephrine 0.3 mg. Within 10 minutes the bronchospasm, urticaria and angioedema had resolved; BP 110/78 mm Hg, HR 90/min, SpO2 97% on 2 L/min oxygen

About 1 h after complete resolution: recurrent generalized urticaria, facial angioedema and chest tightness without stridor or wheeze (BP 110/80 mm Hg, HR 100/min, SpO2 97% on 2 L/min). No further epinephrine; IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and chlorphenamine 10 mg, with resolution within 20 minutes
Admitted for 36 h of observation on IV hydrocortisone 100 mg every 8 h and oral cetirizine 10 mg daily

Discharged with an epinephrine 0.3-mg autoinjector, autoinjector training and an emergency action plan, oral prednisolone 40 mg daily for 5 days, advice to avoid tirzepatide, and outpatient allergy referral
outcome: Remained stable throughout 36 hours of observation and was discharged home with an epinephrine autoinjector and allergy referral; no post-discharge follow-up was available.
teachingPoints: Anaphylaxis is a clinical diagnosis: skin or mucosal signs with respiratory compromise or hypotension minutes after a new drug meet WAO criteria, and treatment must not wait for tryptase or allergy testing.
IM epinephrine (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh is first-line; repeat it after 5 minutes if there is no improvement. Antihistamines, steroids and bronchodilators are adjuncts only.
Persistent respiratory or cardiovascular compromise despite two IM doses is refractory anaphylaxis: start an IV epinephrine infusion with expert help.
Symptoms can recur within hours without re-exposure (biphasic reaction); a severe initial reaction and needing more than one epinephrine dose are risk factors and justify longer observation.

Severe reactions can follow a first known dose in a non-atopic patient; discharge with epinephrine autoinjectors, training, an action plan, trigger avoidance and allergy referral, and send a tryptase level when available.

questions.q: What is the most important first treatment?
options: IM epinephrine 0.3–0.5 mg (1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh
IV chlorphenamine 10 mg with IV hydrocortisone 200 mg
Nebulized albuterol 5 mg, then reassess the blood pressure
IV epinephrine 1 mg bolus (0.1 mg/mL) via a peripheral line
questions.explanation: Hypotension, wheeze and hypoxemia with urticaria and angioedema minutes after a new drug is anaphylaxis, and IM epinephrine into the anterolateral thigh is first-line (EAACI 2021, WAO 2020, Resuscitation Council UK 2021). Antihistamines and steroids do not reverse airway or circulatory compromise, and a 1 mg IV bolus is a cardiac-arrest dose that can cause arrhythmias in a patient with a pulse.

questions.q: What is the most appropriate next step?
questions.extra: 5 minutes after the first IM epinephrine dose and a rapid 1 L saline infusion: BP still 80/50 mm Hg with persistent wheeze.
options: Give IV hydrocortisone and reassess in 30 minutes
Start IV glucagon because epinephrine has failed
Repeat IM epinephrine and continue rapid IV fluids
Intubate before giving any further epinephrine
questions.explanation: If there is no improvement 5 minutes after IM epinephrine, repeat the dose and continue fluid boluses; respiratory or cardiovascular problems that persist after two IM doses define refractory anaphylaxis, which needs an IV epinephrine infusion with expert help (Resuscitation Council UK 2021). Glucagon is for patients on beta-blockers who do not respond to epinephrine.

questions.q: Which feature of her reaction is a recognized risk factor for a biphasic reaction?
questions.extra: Within 10 minutes of a second IM dose: BP 110/78 mm Hg, HR 90/min, SpO2 97% on 2 L/min; rash, angioedema and wheeze resolved.
options: Her long-term use of a combined oral contraceptive
The subcutaneous rather than oral route of the trigger
The absence of prior atopy, asthma or drug allergy
Needing two doses of epinephrine to control the reaction
questions.explanation: A severe initial reaction and the need for more than one epinephrine dose are the best-established risk factors for biphasic anaphylaxis (2020 AAAAI/ACAAI anaphylaxis practice parameter update). Resuscitation Council UK 2021 therefore advises longer observation after resolution when two IM doses were needed; this patient's symptoms recurred about an hour later.

questions.q: Which discharge plan is most appropriate after the observation period?
options: Epinephrine autoinjector with training, action plan, trigger avoidance and allergy referral
Oral antihistamine as needed, and restart tirzepatide at a lower dose
Oral prednisolone alone, since steroids prevent future reactions
No specific measures, because the reaction followed a first dose
questions.explanation: After anaphylaxis, patients should leave with epinephrine autoinjectors and training, a written emergency action plan, advice to avoid the suspected trigger and referral to an allergy specialist (EAACI 2021; Resuscitation Council UK 2021). Steroids and antihistamines do not prevent future anaphylaxis, and reacting to a first dose gives no reassurance about re-exposure.

evidence.quote: A 37-year-old Egyptian woman with a history of migraine and temporomandibular joint disorder presented to the emergency department
a rapid-onset clinical constellation of generalized urticaria, angioedema, and respiratory distress
Approximately 10 minutes prior to symptom onset, she had self-administered her first subcutaneous dose of tirzepatide 2.5 mg into the right side of her abdomen
which had been prescribed by her physician for weight management. The injection pen was new and intact and had been stored correctly.
She denied previous use of tirzepatide or any other GLP-1 receptor agonist.
She denied potential anaphylaxis cofactors, including recent exercise, acute infection, and alcohol consumption. She also denied any new food or medication exposure.
sudden-onset facial and periorbital angioedema, palpitations, nasal congestion, and severe wheezing accompanied by chest tightness
Symptoms rapidly progressed to generalized, pruritic urticarial wheals across her face, trunk, and extremities, accompanied by profound dizziness
Upon arrival at the emergency department, approximately 30 minutes after symptom onset, the patient demonstrated severe hemodynamic compromise and respiratory distress.
a blood pressure (BP) of 80/50 mmHg, a heart rate (HR) of 123 beats/min, a respiratory rate of 24 breaths/min, and an oxygen saturation of 92% on room air
Physical examination demonstrated prominent facial angioedema, widespread urticarial wheals (Figure 1), and diffuse bilateral expiratory wheezing on pulmonary auscultation.
generalized, pruritic urticarial wheals across her face, trunk, and extremities
a mild, non-pruritic, localized 2×2 cm erythematous plaque at the abdominal injection site
a combined oral contraceptive pill (ethinylestradiol 30 mcg/drospirenone 3 mg) for the past five years, alongside intermittent use of esomeprazole 20 mg and ibuprofen 400 mg
She had no history of atopy, bronchial asthma, chronic urticaria, or prior drug allergies.
There was no family history of atopic or immunological diseases.
Diagnostic evaluation, including a 12-lead electrocardiogram and chest radiography, was unremarkable.
White blood cells | 12.86 × 10⁹/L | 4-10 Hemoglobin | 14.2 g/dL
Platelets | 444 × 10⁹/L | 150-400 Urea | 4.6 mmol/L
Creatinine | 59 µmol/L | 44-80 Sodium | 135 mmol/L | 135-145 Potassium | 4.4 mmol/L
Alanine transaminase | 12 U/L | <35 Aspartate aminotransferase | 16 U/L
An acute serum tryptase level was not obtained because testing was unavailable
The patient immediately received a rapid intravenous infusion of 1 L of 0.9% sodium chloride and an initial dose of intramuscular epinephrine 0.3 mg
using a 1 mg/mL (1:1000) solution, administered into the left mid-anterolateral thigh
She also received nebulized albuterol 2.5 mg, ipratropium 0.5 mg, and budesonide 1 mg.
Because hypotension and respiratory compromise persisted after five minutes, a second intramuscular dose of epinephrine 0.3 mg was administered at the same site.
Within 10 minutes of the second epinephrine dose, her respiratory symptoms and cutaneous manifestations had resolved.
Her BP was 110/78 mmHg, her HR was 90 beats per minute, and her oxygen saturation was 97% while receiving oxygen at 2 L/min

Approximately one hour after initial stabilization, while under close observation, the patient developed recurrent generalized urticaria, facial angioedema, and chest tightness. There was no stridor or wheezing.
Her BP remained stable at 110/80 mmHg, her HR was 100 beats per minute, and her oxygen saturation remained 97%
the treating emergency team elected not to administer an additional dose of epinephrine. She was treated with intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg and chlorphenamine 10 mg
after which her symptoms completely resolved within 20 minutes
anaphylaxis was diagnosed clinically according to World Allergy Organization criteria. Tirzepatide was considered the most likely trigger
Given the recurrence of symptoms after complete initial resolution and in the absence of further exposure to the suspected trigger, a biphasic reaction was suspected.
She was maintained on scheduled intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg every eight hours and oral cetirizine 10 mg once daily.
the patient was observed for 36 hours
She remained clinically stable throughout the remainder of her hospital course and was discharged with a prescription for a 0.3-mg epinephrine autoinjector.
The on-call allergy and immunology service provided autoinjector training and an emergency action plan.
prescribed oral prednisolone 40 mg once daily for five days, instructed to avoid any further exposure to tirzepatide, and referred for outpatient allergy and immunology follow-up
no post-discharge follow-up information was available
